\section{Threshold Functions --- Gaussian Polar}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.GaussianPolar
\subsection*{Threshold Functions --- Gaussian Polar: Introduction}
Planar Gaussian density separates into radial and angular factors. Cone masses and the angular overlap of two halfplanes give the geometric formula behind Gaussian quadrant probabilities.

\subsection*{Threshold Functions --- Gaussian Polar: Results}

\begin{definition}[Planar standard Gaussian density]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianDensity2}
\leanok
\statementsource{vershynin-hdp-book}{
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p058-b002,
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p119-b003
}
For $z=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$, the planar Gaussian density is $d_2(x,y)=(2\pi)^{-1}\exp(-(x^2+y^2)/2)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Product of Gaussian densities]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianPDF_mul}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianDensity2}
\proofsource{vershynin-hdp-book}{pdf-681b6f3d947f-p058-b002}
\proofstep
  {BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianDensity2}
  {direct}
  {vershynin-hdp-book}
  {pdf-681b6f3d947f-p058-b002}
\difficulty{4}
For all real numbers $x$ and $y$, the product of the standard Gaussian probability
densities at $x$ and $y$ equals the nonnegative extended real number associated to the
planar standard Gaussian density at $(x,y)$:
$\varphi(x)\varphi(y)=\operatorname{ENNReal}(d_2(x,y))$, where
$d_2(x,y)=(2\pi)^{-1}\exp(-(x^2+y^2)/2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Density of the product Gaussian law]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussian_prod_apply}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianDensity2, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianPDF_mul}
\proofsource{vershynin-hdp-book}{
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p058-b002,
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p119-b003
}
\proofstep
  {BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianDensity2}
  {direct}
  {vershynin-hdp-book}
  {pdf-681b6f3d947f-p058-b002}
\proofstep
  {BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianPDF_mul}
  {direct}
  {vershynin-hdp-book}
  {pdf-681b6f3d947f-p058-b002}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\gamma$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For every
measurable set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, the product measure $\gamma\otimes\gamma$
assigns $A$ the nonnegative extended real integral of the planar standard Gaussian
density: $(\gamma\otimes\gamma)(A)=\int_A d_2(x,y)\,d(x,y)$, where
$d_2(x,y)=(2\pi)^{-1}\exp(-(x^2+y^2)/2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Radial Gaussian normalization]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.lintegral_radial}
\leanok
\difficulty{5}
The nonnegative extended integral of $r\exp(-r^2/2)$ over $r>0$ equals $1$:
$\displaystyle\int_{(0,\infty)} r\exp(-r^2/2)\,dr=1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Gaussian mass of a cone]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussian_cone_lintegral}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.gaussianDensity2, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.lintegral_radial}
\difficulty{6}
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R$ be measurable. Suppose that
for every $r>0$ and every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\in A$ if and
only if $\theta\in\Theta$. Then the integral of the planar standard Gaussian density
over $A$, interpreted as a nonnegative extended real integral, is $(2\pi)^{-1}$ times
the Lebesgue measure of $\Theta\cap(-\pi,\pi)$: $\int_A
d_2(x,y)\,d(x,y)=(2\pi)^{-1}\,\operatorname{Leb}(\Theta\cap(-\pi,\pi))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Nonpositive cosine on a centered period]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.cos_nonpos_iff_of_mem_Ioo}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real number $\theta$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, one has $\cos\theta\le0$ if and
only if $\theta\le-\pi/2$ or $\pi/2\le\theta$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Cosine sign on a negative angular interval]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.cos_nonpos_iff_of_le_neg_pi_div_two}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real $u$ satisfying $-2\pi<u\le-\pi/2$, one has $\cos u\le0$ if and only if
$-3\pi/2\le u$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Nonpositive cosine with a closed left endpoint]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.cos_nonpos_iff_of_neg_pi_div_two_le}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real number $u$ with $-\pi/2\le u<\pi$, one has $\cos u\le0$ if and only if
$\pi/2\le u$ or $u=-\pi/2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Measurability of a two-half-plane angle set]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.measurableSet_twoHalfplaneAngles}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $\alpha$, the set $\{\theta\in\mathbb R : \cos\theta\le 0 \text{
and } \cos(\theta-\alpha)\le 0\}$ is measurable.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Angular overlap of two halfplanes]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.angular_measure_two_halfplanes}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.cos_nonpos_iff_of_le_neg_pi_div_two, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.cos_nonpos_iff_of_mem_Ioo, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.cos_nonpos_iff_of_neg_pi_div_two_le, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.measurableSet_twoHalfplaneAngles}
\difficulty{6}
For every real $\alpha$ with $0\le\alpha\le\pi$, the Lebesgue measure of the angles
$\theta\in(-\pi,\pi)$ satisfying both $\cos\theta\le0$ and $\cos(\theta-\alpha)\le0$ is
$\pi-\alpha$.
\end{lemma}
